Yet another made the case for the traditional version in all its canned glory: "[The mushier] the better with canned green beans."

articles.title: Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office
articles.summary: It comes a month after opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to Venezuela.
articles.body:
Venezuela will repeal a law that prohibits opposition figures from office, National Assembly Chief Jorge Rodriguez has announced.

The legislation, approved in 2024 and criticised for enabling political persecution, targeted those who promoted or supported sanctions against the country.

“That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through,” Rodriguez said on Thursday.

The law was passed just after fraught elections which the then-incumbent Nicolas Maduro ultimately won amid widespread allegations of fraud.

An interim government headed by Delcy Rodriguez, the parliamentary chief’s sister, has run Venezuela since Maduro’s abduction by US forces in January. Delcy Rodriguez promised in September during a speech at the United Nations that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.

Since then, the US-backed government has been in political transition talks with parts of the opposition selected by Washington. That dialogue had reached an agreement to review several laws, including the one up for repeal now, according to Jorge Rodriguez.

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado shook up Venezuelan politics with her surprise return from exile last month . Machado won an opposition primary in 2023 to take on Maduro in the following year’s election, but she was legally barred from running. The Nobel Peace Prize laureate is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election, despite her exclusion from transition talks.

Despite being shut out, on Thursday Machado launched a system of neighbourhood assemblies aiming to gather proposals for a future government programme and democratic transition. The assemblies are expected to bring together over a million people over several months, according to Machado’s team.

“We listened to neighbours who are breaking down barriers that many thought were impossible, debating the issues that will lay the foundations for the Venezuela to come,” Machado said on social media on Thursday after the meetings. “We are designing the transition to democracy, the Venezuelan way.”

Around 2,000 meetings with residents were organised in Venezuela and abroad on the first day of the initiative, her team told the AFP news agency.

Nineteen questions are asked during the assembly, with responses fed into a digital platform. Issues of national interest range from dates for the presidential election to changes in the justice, education, health, wage and pension systems, as well as the role of the public and private sectors.

articles.title: California records something never before confirmed on the US West Coast as two olive ridley sea turtle nests produce more than 70 hatchlings
articles.summary: California has recorded an unprecedented wildlife event after two olive ridley sea turtles laid eggs on beaches along the state's coast, marking the first
articles.body: California has recorded an unprecedented wildlife event after two olive ridley sea turtles laid eggs on beaches along the state's coast, marking the first confirmed natural sea turtle nests on the US West Coast. The nests were discovered in September 2026 at Seal Beach and Huntington Beach, surprising researchers who had not previously documented the species nesting in the region. With high tides and approaching tropical storms threatening the eggs, an inter-agency team moved them to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach for protection. The eggs later hatched, producing 75 baby turtles. The hatchlings were subsequently released into the Pacific Ocean in November, turning an unexpected discovery into a significant milestone for marine conservation.Two olive ridley sea turtles make history with first confirmed West Coast nestsThe first olive ridley sea turtle was observed digging a nest and laying eggs at Seal Beach in Orange County on September 16. Three days later, another turtle was spotted nesting near the Huntington Beach Pier, around eight miles away.The discoveries marked the first recorded instances of natural sea turtle nesting on the US West Coast. Olive ridley turtles are generally associated with tropical and warm waters across the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, with major nesting populations found in countries including Mexico, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama.Researchers used photographic identification to study the two turtles. The discovery prompted local, state and federal agencies to work together to monitor and protect the nests.More than 200 eggs moved to safetyThe nesting sites faced the threat of high surf and rising tides as tropical storms approached the California coast. Wildlife officials and biologists decided to relocate the eggs to prevent the nests from being washed away.On September 25, an inter-agency team collected 204 eggs from the two beaches and transported them to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach. The eggs were placed in incubators under sand inside a secure facility, where aquarium staff monitored temperature and humidity throughout the incubation period.Olive ridley eggs typically take between 45 and 60 days to hatch. The aquarium's animal care team monitored their development while working with federal and local partners.75 hatchlings make their way into the PacificThe first successful hatching took place in November. On November 14, 54 olive ridley hatchlings from the Seal Beach nest were released into the ocean near the location where their eggs had originally been laid.A second group followed the next morning. On November 15, another 21 hatchlings from the Huntington Beach nest were released near their original nesting site. Together, the two releases brought the number of baby turtles entering the Pacific to 75.The hatchlings were transported from the aquarium back to the beaches and placed on the sand, allowing them to crawl towards the ocean. Aquarium staff and wildlife partners carried out the releases during the early morning hours.Could El Niño have brought the turtles north?Scientists are examining whether unusually warm ocean conditions helped the olive ridley turtles reach California. A strong El Niño and an extreme marine heatwave pushed Southern California's water temperatures closer to those found in the turtles' usual nesting grounds.The Aquarium of the Pacific said the unusual nesting behaviour may have been influenced by changing weather patterns, the approaching El Niño, a recent tropical storm, natural range expansion or navigational errors. The precise reason the turtles selected these beaches remains unknown.The discovery has raised questions about whether olive ridleys could begin nesting farther north more frequently. Researchers are continuing to monitor the coastline for additional nesting activity.A difficult journey lies ahead for the hatchlingsReaching the ocean is only the beginning of the young turtles' struggle to survive. Once in the water, olive ridley hatchlings must avoid predators, find food and navigate towards deeper waters. They swim continuously for several days as they move away from the shoreline.Their chances of reaching adulthood are extremely low. The Aquarium of the Pacific estimates that only around one in 1,000 olive ridley hatchlings survives to adulthood.The aquarium and its partners have urged people to watch for further sea turtle activity along Southern California beaches and report sightings to local lifeguards or wildlife authorities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Steelers and Broncos players sending Aaron Rodgers signs through their scoring play celebrations
articles.summary: DK Metcalf held up eight fingers after scoring for the Steelers, while Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton imitated Aaron Rodgers "Discount Double Check."
articles.body: After much was made of Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers this week, an actual game began between the quarterback's former team and the Denver Broncos on Friday. And some players from both teams made their scores about, you guessed it, Aaron Rodgers. AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY DISAGREEMENTS AT HEART OF QUARTERBACK'S BENCHING BY THE STEELERS The Steelers took a surprising 14-0 lead in the first quarter, with the second of their scores coming on a 22-yard pass from new starting quarterback Mason Rudolph to DK Metcalf. And after the score, Metcalf made a couple of hand signals as part of his celebration. One of those was Metcalf holding up four fingers on each hand. As in 8. That was Rodgers' number in Pittsburgh before he was released on Wednesday. Several people on social media who apparently read sign language translated Metcalf's signing to mean: "Stand on business, 8." In the second quarter, the Broncos scored their first points of the game when Alex Singleton tackled Jaylen Warren in the end zone for a safety. That has become the biggest story in the NFL this week. It's clear players in the Steelers' locker room, such as Metcalf, are not going to soon forget their former leader. articles.title: A 15-foot Burmese python weighing 134 pounds was found hiding in front-yard bushes during a late-night dog walk in a Florida neighbourhood near Naples
articles.summary: A routine late-night dog walk turned into a startling wildlife encounter for a Florida couple after a huge Burmese python was found hiding in bushes near
articles.body: A routine late-night dog walk turned into a startling wildlife encounter for a Florida couple after a huge Burmese python was found hiding in bushes near a home in a residential community southeast of Naples. The snake was discovered on November 6 in Chase Preserve, part of Lely Resort, after a neighbour first spotted it near a sidewalk and alerted residents. By around 10 pm, several people had gathered around the landscaping where the python was hiding. A professional trapper was called to the scene and removed the enormous female snake in about three minutes.Florida couple found 15-foot Burmese python during late-night dog walkThe encounter began when a resident walking with her husband spotted a large snake near the sidewalk on Celeste Drive. She recorded the animal and shared the footage with Kristen Bowerman through the neighbourhood's group messaging app, according to the report by Naples Daily News.About an hour later, at roughly 10 pm, Bowerman and her husband, Scott, took their dog outside for its final walk of the night. They soon noticed several neighbours gathered near bushes beside a nearby home. The snake had been located in the landscaping, prompting residents to stop and watch as they waited for professional help.Scott moved closer to record the encounter while Kristen kept their dog away from the snake. The reptile was eventually identified as a Burmese python, a large constrictor that is established as an invasive species in South Florida.The size of the animal became clear once it was removed from the bushes. The female python measured 15 feet 2 inches long and weighed 134 pounds, making it substantially larger than the adult Burmese pythons commonly encountered in Florida.Trapper hauled 134-pound female python out of the bushes in three minutesProfessional wildlife trapper Kenne Helm, who operates as Trapper Helm, responded to the residential sighting. According to the AOL report, Helm entered the bushes where the snake was hiding and managed to capture it in approximately three minutes.The python was then measured and weighed, confirming its length of 15 feet 2 inches and weight of 134 pounds. The snake was female, and Helm believed it may have been moving through the area during the seasonal reproductive period in search of a mate before nesting.The capture ended an unusual night for residents, but the snake was not released. The reports said the python was humanely euthanised after being captured, with its remains subsequently given to a python biologist for research.The incident also drew attention because the snake was found in a residential neighbourhood rather than a remote area. Its hiding place in landscaped bushes meant it was close to homes and people before residents realised what was there.Why Burmese pythons are a major invasive species problem in FloridaBurmese pythons are not native to Florida and originated in parts of Asia. The species became established in South Florida after captive animals escaped or were released, eventually developing a reproducing wild population.The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission considers Burmese pythons an established invasive species across a substantial part of South Florida. The range reported by the sources extends from areas south of Lake Okeechobee towards Key Largo and westward into parts of Broward and Collier counties.Most Burmese pythons captured in Florida are considerably smaller than the Chase Preserve specimen. The reports said captured adults commonly measure around six to 10 feet, making the 15-foot, 2-inch female an unusually large example.Their size is significant because Burmese pythons are powerful constrictors that prey on mammals, birds and reptiles. Their presence can put pressure on native wildlife, while large snakes found close to homes can also create concerns for residents with dogs and other pets.What happened to the giant Burmese python after it was captured?After the 134-pound python was removed, its remains were handed to a python biologist for research. According to the reports, the scientific examination could provide information about the animal and the invasive population in South Florida.Helm's company also participates in a volunteer response programme that helps Collier County residents remove large invasive constrictors without charging them for the service, according to the reports.The encounter highlights how an invasive Burmese python can turn up in an ordinary residential setting. For the Chase Preserve residents, what began as a warning about a snake near a sidewalk ended with neighbours gathered around a front-yard bush and a professional trapper pulling a 15-foot female python from the landscaping.You use AI every day. articles.title: Princess Kate wants people to learn from her cancer journey in vulnerable new documentary
articles.summary: LONDON — Catherine, Princess of Wales, reveals how cancer treatment terrified and changed her in a very personal documentary she said she hopes will help others reckon with the disease.
articles.body: LONDON — Catherine, Princess of Wales, reveals how cancer treatment terrified and changed her in a very personal documentary she said she hopes will help others reckon with the disease. In “Heal,” the royal reflects on mortality with an openness and vulnerability that breaks with the royals’ trademark stoicism and reserve, describing the human challenges she faces after her treatment. The normally private princess gives viewers a glimpse — albeit a highly controlled one — of her cancer journey in the 30-minute film, which was produced to raise money for the Royal Marsden Hospital in London, where she received chemotherapy. The film marks a change in the way royals have spoken about their personal lives. “William and Kate are communicating more directly with the public than ever before and being more open emotionally than we’ve ever seen,” said Emily Nash, NBC News’ royal contributor. “That really, I think, is as a result of her cancer diagnosis. It’s really changed their lives and they want to share what they’ve learned with the world.” Speaking in London at a special screening of the documentary that will air on NBC on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on Peacock from Dec. 1, Kate told reporters that cancer “doesn’t just affect the body. It changes how you think and feel and profoundly affects every aspect of life.” “I know this personally, and that the journey through and beyond treatment requires more than medicine alone,” she said. In the film, Kate explains how cancer changed her. “Once you experience something like that, it’s very hard to go back to the person you were before,” she says. “Something like cancer strips everything away,” added Kate, who has made cancer support a central part of her work since her illness. “Yes, it’s physical, but it’s emotional too. The things you thought you knew are no longer there. And you do, in a way, lose yourself.” Rugged British landscapes play a central role in the film. It was simply shot and accompanied by a score by Scottish composer Erland Cooper, who drew inspiration from birdsong and the natural world. The documentary “also carries with it a deeper message,” she added. “Healing, whether personal or collective, is not just about fixing what is wrong. It is about finding balance in how we live. Between effort and acceptance, between control and trust, between thinking and simply being.” Kate had already broken with royal tradition when revealing her diagnosis and subsequent remission. Rather than issuing a traditional text statement, she announced she was receiving treatment for the disease in a three-minute video. Alongside her family, in a sepia-toned follow-up video featuring mellow music, cinematic angles and slow-motion effects, Kate later announced her return to royal duties. The royals have invited cameras into their lives before, notably in 1969’s “Royal Family” documentary, which showed Queen Elizabeth II behind the scenes, but kept their distance through formality. Kate’s brother- and sister-in-law produced the six-part Netflix documentary series “Harry & Meghan” after they stepped down as working royals. Both then and now in her latest documentary, Kate has not revealed what type of cancer she was diagnosed with in March 2024 after major abdominal surgery, but in “Heal” she says that the disease changed her. Talking about her time in the hospital, she says in the film that it was “a really scary, disorientating experience.” On one occasion, she says, the simple act of someone holding her hand made all the difference. “I think I was sort of in and out of consciousness. It was a really dark time. But also then, somewhere through that too, I became aware of someone holding my hand. They weren’t talking to me. They weren’t trying to fix anything. They were just there. And the presence of someone that stood by me in that time, I’ll forever be grateful for,” she says. Although she is seen crying at one point when she hears messages of support from her three children, George, Charlotte and Louis, there are also lighter moments. Part of the film shows Kate completing what is known as the National Three Peaks Challenge, in which she scaled Scafell Pike, Ben Nevis and Snowdon, the highest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales, in just 24 hours. At one point, she plays a game of “Would you rather” with her brother James as they walk, challenging him to pick between two funny and difficult options. She told him she played the game with her children. Along their journey, she also met up with some hikers and spoke to other people about the challenges they faced fighting cancer. “You don’t get any help with that from doctors or the language that they use,” one told her. “There are no tools in the clinical settings to kind of help with that. Finding language or finding other people, that community or art or something, these are the only tools we have, I think, to explain and to exercise your uncertainty and become OK with it.” The film makes no mention of King Charles III, who revealed his own cancer diagnosis in February 2024, a month before Kate. But the princess said ahead of the film’s release that she hoped it would “encourage compassion, showing the real value in standing alongside one another in the hardest of times.” “Above all, I hope it helps support the life-changing work of the Royal Marsden and all those navigating life with cancer to ensure no one faces this disease feeling unseen, unsupported or alone.”

articles.title: US military says it disabled merchant ship trying to breach Iran blockade
articles.summary: The US military says it disabled the Palau-flagged ship’s propulsion but its crew was unharmed.
articles.body:
The US military says it has fired on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman and claims it was trying to breach an American blockade on Iranian ports.

Military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the “ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed”, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement.

US officials say the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel’s destination as Singapore. It is at least the 15th vessel the US military has publicly acknowledged disabling since the blockade began in April, and the sixth since it resumed it in July. The previous vessel was disabled on November 7.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an “unauthorised” route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.

The claims could not be independently verified.

The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said on Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations “that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region’s waters”.

The US military has maintained a sizeable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.

American ships have been blockading Iranian ports since April, although the blockade was temporarily lifted during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the US military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabled those that refuse to comply.

CENTCOM, which has its headquarters in Florida, has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.

articles.title: A Wisconsin wife signed a prenup two days before her 2006 wedding that promised $350,000 after 15 years of marriage; 20 years later, judges rejected the deal as her husband's income exceeded $81,000 a month
articles.summary: A marriage contract designed to protect a family business resulted in a prolonged divorce battle in Wisconsin after a judge ruled the financial
articles.body: A marriage contract designed to protect a family business resulted in a prolonged divorce battle in Wisconsin after a judge ruled the financial arrangement was less than fair. Almost 20 years after signing the document, a woman won an appellate ruling overturning its enforcement amid a dramatic increase in her ex-husband’s wealth and questions about what financial information she knew before the marriage.The Wisconsin Court of Appeals ruled that Ryan David Chernick and Tracy Marie Chernick signed their marital property agreement on Feb. 23, 2006, two days before they were married. The agreement promised Tracy a lump-sum payment of $350,000 if they stayed married for 15 years or more and had children together.A prenup signed days before the weddingThe deal was intended mainly to protect Ryan’s financial interests, especially his stake in Camera Corner, a family business started by his grandfather.Court records showed Ryan’s financial disclosure listed an estimated net worth of more than $2.25 million, including a 10% ownership stake in the company worth about $400,000. But the deal did not disclose the overall value of the business, or an estimate of how much Ryan could make taking over from his father.Meanwhile, Tracy reported a net worth of roughly negative $5,700 and an annual income of just over $6,000.The Wisconsin Court of Appeals acknowledged that Tracy had legal representation during the negotiations, but significant questions remained about whether she had been provided enough information to understand the financial impact of signing the agreement.Husband's income increased dramaticallyThe couple’s finances changed dramatically in the next few years. Ryan eventually moved into management at Camera Corner, which was then acquired by a larger company that bought his shares.His adjusted gross income was nearly $1.2 million in 2019, more than $450,000 in 2020, more than $800,000 in 2021 and more than $1 million in both 2022 and 2023.The Wisconsin Court of Appeals said Ryan reported a monthly income of $81,694 at the time of the divorce. It was more than 16 times what Tracy thought he made before they got married.When Ryan filed for divorce in 2022, Tracy challenged the validity of the agreement.Judges say financial disclosure not enoughThe Wisconsin Court of Appeals said Ryan didn’t disclose important information about the growth expected for Camera Corner and what Ryan’s income would be when he took over for his dad.The court also found that Tracy could not have reasonably anticipated the level of the family's ultimate wealth at the time she signed the agreement.Wisconsin law requires marital property agreements to meet requirements for financial disclosure, voluntary consent and substantive fairness. The Court of Appeal found that the agreement did not pass the requirements for financial disclosure and fairness.It therefore ruled that the agreement was not binding in the division of the couple's assets.Divorce settlement returned for re-examinationThe financial support Tracy was entitled to after the divorce was also part of the appellate decision.The lower court ordered Ryan to pay maintenance between $4,000 and $12,000 a month over seven years, plus a $239,799.17 property equalization payment.But the Wisconsin Court of Appeals said the arrangement could leave Tracy short of money to meet her expenses when maintenance ends. It ordered the lower court to reexamine the division of property and the maintenance award.The decision of November 24, 2026, reversed the judgment of divorce in part and remanded the case for further proceedings.The ruling leaves the door open to reexamining the financial settlement between the couple, with the court calling for a fairer assessment of the wealth generated during their marriage.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.title: Kenyan cult leader guilty of manslaughter more than 123 starvation deaths
articles.summary: Paul Mackenzie, already serving 200 years, is the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.
articles.body:
A Kenyan court has found cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction for Mackenzie, the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.

Mackenzie was convicted on Friday in the coastal city of Mombasa, along with 29 followers, including his wife, Rhoda Mumbua.

Magistrate Alex Ithuku said Mackenzie “gave the directions to fast to death”, Reuters reported. Mackenzie pleaded not guilty, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing.

On November 6, Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, 190 of them children. He had denied forcing the victims to starve, but the court rejected his defence.

He was also convicted this week of child cruelty, assault, radicalisation and “terrorism-related offences”, according to Reuters. He is due to be sentenced on the child cruelty and radicalisation charges in December, The Associated Press reported.

Mackenzie led the Good News International Church in the Shakahola Forest, near Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast.

He told followers to starve themselves and their children to death to meet Jesus before the end of the world.

Police arrested him in 2023 after a tip-off, and authorities began uncovering more than 400 bodies . People familiar with the cult told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the starvation in three phases : children first, then women and young men, and finally, the remaining men.

Mackenzie had been arrested twice before, in connection with the deaths of children, and released.

The killings have shocked Kenya and led to calls for tighter oversight of religious groups.

President William Ruto said in 2023 that he took responsibility as head of state for the government’s failure to prevent the deaths.

Other mass killings linked to cults include one in Uganda in 2000, when a doomsday group killed more than 700 people, and the 1978 massacre in Guyana, where an American cult leader ordered more than 900 followers to drink poison, Reuters said.

articles.title: 'We've released our debut album - nearly 40 years after it was recorded'
articles.summary: The Catburgers will finally perform songs from their album Galashiels in the town it was named after.
articles.body:
An Edinburgh band have reformed after decades to finally release their debut album that was recorded in the 1980s.

The Catburgers have named the nine upbeat songs after the town where they played their favourite gig of the time - Galashiels.

Stuart Macgregor, Robert Jones, Jeff Duffy and Keith Burns were rising stars of the Scottish music scene, regularly headlining shows in London, Glasgow and Aberdeen.

University graduations and job offers led to them splitting up in 1990 - months before their album was due for release.

Singer and guitarist Robert Jones said: "I don't think in hindsight we were driven and committed enough to being hugely successful - we were a bit too laid-back."

During the mid-to-late 1980s The Catburgers were one of Edinburgh's most prominent live bands, sharing stages with the likes of Primal Scream, Television Personalities and the Wedding Present.

However, just months after recording their highly anticipated debut album in 1989 for the London label Dreamworld Records, they split up.

Although the collection of songs - which featured fans' favourites such as I've Got a Friend, Children's TV and The First Day of Spring - was never released, drummer Jeff Duffy kept hold of the master tapes.

In 2023, with retirement approaching, deputy head teacher Jones had the tapes digitised at a studio in Glasgow.

"I have never been one to think about what could have happened but my son found some of our demo tapes in the attic a few years ago and liked them, the 61-year-old said.

"That led to me getting the album master tapes back from Jeff and here we are today - reformed and ready to play the songs again."

The recent death of Duffy, and other musical commitments of guitarist Burns, led to two new members - Dave Paul and Johnny Allan - being recruited.

Within a few months of getting back together, US label Slumberdown Records offered to release the long-delayed debut album.

The Catburgers decided on Galashiels for the LP's name in honour of their favourite gig from the 1980s.

Jones said: "We hadn't got as far as naming the album back in the 80s when we recorded it - then I just remembered the story of our gig in Galashiels at the college of textiles and it just felt right.

"It was winter time - a dark, wild night - and Jeff, our sadly departed drummer, started playing at half speed as he was coming down with a bug.

"We played this whole set really slowly as far as we were concerned, and we were a bit in the dark about how we were going down.

"We came off stage at the end of the night and the crowd were so positive - they were buzzing, telling us how amazing they thought we were - that always stuck with us as being a kind of a high point in The Catburgers story. "

Having already played a handful of warm-up gigs in Edinburgh, the band are now set to return to Galashiels to play their album in the town it was named after.

Bass player and chemistry lecturer Macgregor is enjoying being back on the stage and cannot wait to play in the Borders once more.

The 60-year-old said: "When I stopped playing with The Catburgers, I did a little bit in the early 1990s but then I literally put the bass under the bed where it stayed until recently.

"Picking up the bass again after all that time was a real reinvention - but I knew that once upon a time I used to be able to play this stuff.

"There has been a lot of enthusiasm for the album since its recent release and obviously for the band as well, so it is great to be back."

Although drummer Allan is a new member of the band, the 58-year-old children's charity worker was a fan of the original group.

"The Catburgers were regulars at the Onion Cellar club that I used to go to when I was 18 or 19," he said.

"Their music always felt kind of edgy and they were always hugely entertaining live.

"I wish I'd played with them when I was a teenager - when I had the energy for it - but it's still great fun and I'm really enjoying it."

The band will play at the MacArts venue in Galashiels on 19 December with support from local Borders bands.

Venue manager Chris Wemyss said: "As soon as we heard about the remarkable story of the Galashiels album we just had to have The Catburgers along to play at the MacArts.

"Many of our regulars won't have been born when these songs were first recorded but they sound as fresh today as they did back in the 80s."

articles.title: Will Taiwan vote to revive nuclear power – and why does that matter for AI?
articles.summary: Voters will decide on Saturday whether to scrap the country’s ‘nuclear-free homeland’ policy.
articles.body:
Voters in Taiwan are set to decide whether to bring back nuclear power – 18 months after its last operational reactor was shut down.

A referendum on the issue is being held alongside local elections on Saturday. It is the island’s fourth vote on nuclear power in just eight years.

It comes as demand for electricity to fuel the country’s burgeoning computer chip industry soars and concern grows about how Taiwan would keep its lights on if China, which claims the island as its own territory, cut it off amid escalating tensions.

Voters are being asked whether the government should return to using nuclear power to boost the economy. That would mean abolishing the country’s longstanding “nuclear-free homeland” policy.

The opposition Kuomintang (KMT) proposed the referendum and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is also backing it. The legislature approved the referendum in August and the Central Election Commission signed it off on August 28.

To pass, ‘yes’ votes must outnumber ‘no’ votes and exceed a quarter of all eligible voters.

The ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), which has long had a policy of no nuclear power in its mandate, is urging ‘no’. DPP legislator Chen Pei-yu called the referendum unnecessary, saying lawmakers could change the policy by amending existing laws instead.

Taiwan once relied heavily on nuclear power. In 1985, its three plants produced 52 percent of the nation’s electricity.

Nuclear power then became one of the most partisan issues in Taiwanese politics. Lev Nachman, an assistant professor at the Graduate Institute of National Development at National Taiwan University, said the divide goes back to the DPP’s founding.

“There was a major group of environmentalists that were part of the party that were very anti-nuclear,” Nachman told Al Jazeera. The nuclear industry, by contrast, was built and run under the KMT.

Polarisation turned that into “a very green-versus-blue issue”, Nachman said, referring to the colours of the DPP and the KMT.

Safety fears run deep. Nachman said Taiwan watched the 2011 Fukushima nuclear plant meltdown in neighbouring Japan very closely.

“There is this sort of fear of any sort of nuclear reaction that would ever happen in Taiwan would just devastate the entire island,” he said. Active geological fault lines run across Taiwan and the question of how to dispose of nuclear waste remains unresolved.

The DPP has governed since 2016, partly on a pledge to phase out nuclear power. In May last year, Taiwan shut down its last reactor at Maanshan in Pingtung County.

Why is nuclear power back on the agenda?

Public opinion has been mixed in three previous referendums. In 2018, voters opted to scrap a legal deadline for phasing out nuclear power. But in 2021, they rejected restarting construction on an unfinished fourth nuclear plant. In August last year, a majority vote to restart the Maanshan plant was voided due to low turnout.

Now, nuclear power is back on the agenda because surging electricity demand from Taiwan’s semiconductor and AI industries, along with growing fears about energy security and over-reliance on imported fuel, have renewed the debate over how the island keeps the lights on in an emergency.

According to the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Taiwan imports more than 97 percent of its energy. Natural gas generates about 43 percent of its electricity and coal about 35 percent. Both arrive by ship.

Taiwan only has about 11 days of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in reserve. Japan and South Korea hold between 14 and 20 days.

“There’s two sides to it,” Nachman said. The first is energy security: “If China actually blockades Taiwan and cuts off access to the outside world, then Taiwan only has so much energy it can rely on.”

The second is the chip industry, which requires huge amounts of power and “that’s only going to increase over time”, he said.

The war with Iran this year has added to the pressure by disrupting LNG shipments from the Middle East.

Will the ruling party change its stance?

The DPP has already started to shift. In March, President William Lai Ching-te said the government would begin the process of restarting the Maanshan and Kuosheng plants. He cited AI-driven demand and conflicts abroad causing disruption to energy supplies.

On September 24, the Nuclear Safety Commission approved state-owned Taipower’s restart plan for Maanshan. Further safety assessments are still needed before it can operate again.

Nachman said Lai has tried to push his party to rethink its “very dogmatic anti-nuclear stance”. The question is whether DPP voters have come around.

Nuclear power is not Taiwan’s first choice for filling the gap, however. “Investment in LNG – that’s still Taiwan’s kind of number one goal,” Nachman said.

How important is Taiwan’s microchip industry?

Taiwan is the most important link in the global AI supply chain.

It makes more than 90 percent of the world’s most advanced semiconductors, nearly all of them at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). TSMC has more than 60 percent of the global contract chipmaking market.

Its customers include Nvidia – the world’s most valuable semiconductor company – AMD and Apple. TSMC makes Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin AI processors, and Taiwanese firms such as Foxconn and Quanta build most of the world’s AI servers.

That uses huge amounts of electricity and water. In September, Taiwan’s semiconductor industry used more than 4.5 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity for the first time. That was up 11.55 percent from a year earlier, driven by AI demand.

S&P Global estimated that TSMC alone used about 8 percent of Taiwan’s electricity in 2023. That share could rise to almost 24 percent by 2030, it added.

Nachman cautioned against seeing the referendum only through the demand for microchips and semiconductors. “In today’s media, Taiwan has become a single issue, just about semiconductors,” he said. “For a lot of people in Taiwan, the semiconductors aren’t even the priority. It really is the security side.”

Will China object to Taiwan having nuclear power?

Probably not. Beijing does not appear to have commented on the referendum itself.

“The nuclear issue is a completely separate issue from anything related to China,” Nachman said. “It’s much more a matter of domestic politics.”

China has, however, used Taiwan’s energy weakness in its messaging. In March, Chen Binhua, a spokesman for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said closer integration with China could help solve Taiwan’s energy problems. He pointed to the island’s reliance on oil and gas from the Middle East.

Taipei rejects unification with Beijing. Analysts writing in The Diplomat called the offer an exercise in optics.

However, it remains a top priority for China. During a speech in Beijing on November 12, President Xi Jinping once again stated that Taiwan and China must be reunified.

The referendum is about civilian power reactors, not weapons. Asked whether Taiwan might seek a nuclear weapon, Nachman said: “No, of course not. This is just about nuclear power.”

Taiwan did secretly pursue nuclear weapons in the 1970s and 1980s. The programme was shut down in 1988 under US pressure, after a senior nuclear scientist, Chang Hsien-yi, defected to the United States.

Since then, Taiwan’s leaders have consistently stated that they will not seek nuclear weapons. Its nuclear facilities are inspected under an arrangement between Taiwan, the US and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

The bigger worry is a blockade by China if it seeks to press reunification in the future. Nachman said large military drills and naval patrols China has held around Taiwan since US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit in 2022 have all rehearsed one.

Will the referendum pass and what happens next?

Nachman said he is sceptical. “We keep doing it over and over again and it still doesn’t usually pass,” he said. “So my expectations are actually fairly low.”

The outcome will depend on DPP supporters. “It’s really more a matter of whether or not green voters have come around to it,” Nachman said.

If the referendum does pass, he said Lai and the DPP “would probably be largely okay with it”.

The restart process is already under way either way. Supporters say reactors could be running again within 18 months to three years. Opponents say a restart could take five to 10 years and cost several hundred billion New Taiwan dollars.

articles.title: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum protests new DEA tip line for reporting criminals, corrupt officials
articles.summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico filed a formal complaint over the DEA tip line that lets anonymous callers report cartel operatives.
articles.body: Mexico has filed a formal complaint with the United States over a new Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) tip line that allows anonymous callers to report corrupt government officials and cartel operatives, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday. Sheinbaum, who has repeatedly pushed back against U. S. actions targeting Mexican drug cartels, announced the diplomatic protest during her daily morning briefing. "We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," she said. DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK The Trump administration has argued that Mexico has not done enough to combat cartels or stem the flow of fentanyl into the United States, while Sheinbaum has accused Washington of infringing on Mexican sovereignty. "The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said Thursday. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups." COAST GUARD FIREFIGHT PUTS US, MEXICO AT ODDS DESPITE COORDINATED BORDER OPERATIONS On Wednesday, DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the launch of the tip line, saying anonymous callers could report members and associates of designated terrorist organizations, corrupt officials who benefit from them, criminal networks and money launderers financing narco-terrorism in the Mexican state of Sinaloa, home to the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the country's most powerful and violent drug trafficking groups. FOLLOW US ON X Cole added that phone numbers for a similar tip line targeting the state of Jalisco would be released later. DOJ FLOODED WITH THOUSANDS OF FRAUD TIPS AFTER CASH INCENTIVE LAUNCH, TRUMP OFFICIAL SAYS Sheinbaum urged Washington to focus on curbing drug use and cartel activity within its own borders, adding that Mexico would continue to confront criminal organizations to prevent drugs from reaching the United States. GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS "The United States has a responsibility to its people to address drug use, as well as to arrest members of the drug cartels operating in the United States," Sheinbaum said. "We cannot have this view that the responsibility lies with Mexico." EXCLUSIVE: FENTANYL DEATHS PLUNGE 22% AS TRUMP WHITE HOUSE TOUTS CRACKDOWN ON DEADLY DRUG CRISIS Her remarks came days after Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," an ally of a Sinaloa Cartel faction, was captured in Mexico during a joint U.S.-Mexican operation. The State Department had previously offered a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest. GOT A TIP? Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House and the DEA for comment. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: US pushed Venezuela, Iraq to quit OPEC to boost oil output: Report
articles.summary: The United States pushed Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year.
articles.body: The United States pushed Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC earlier this year. Washington even blocked Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues to the oil producers' group, a Reuters report said, citing 10 people familiar with the matter.The moves were aimed at two of OPEC's five founding members and reflected the Trump administration's efforts to boost oil production and prevent the group's output limits from restricting US energy ambitions.The US pressure on Venezuela was strong enough to prompt Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to intervene this summer. He persuaded the Trump administration not to pursue the issue further, two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters.In Iraq, Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi raised the possibility of leaving OPEC at a government meeting this summer after discussions with US officials who encouraged the move. However, Iraq's oil ministry opposed the idea and persuaded him to remain in the group. It suggested that Baghdad could instead seek a higher production quota, the sources said.The developments come as US oil companies look to expand their investments in both countries. Washington was concerned that OPEC's production limits could eventually restrict plans to increase output, according to people familiar with the discussions.US used financial leverage over VenezuelaAfter the US removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, the State Department opened discussions with Venezuelan officials in Washington on whether the country should leave OPEC, five people familiar with the matter told Reuters.The Trump administration wanted US oil majors to revive Venezuela's oil production. Trump had argued that higher output would strengthen energy security in the Western Hemisphere. However, officials feared that OPEC's production policies could stand in the way of those plans.Washington also prevented Venezuela from paying its annual OPEC membership dues, according to people familiar with the matter. The US controls Venezuela's access to state funds following Maduro's removal.The State Department did not directly answer questions about blocking the payment. However, it confirmed that Washington has authority over Venezuela's use of state funds held in a US-controlled account."The Department receives disbursement requests from the interim Venezuelan government and reviews the requests, including against a list of approved and prohibited uses of the foreign Government Deposit Funds," a State Department official told Reuters.The official said lower-level US officials may have raised the possibility of Venezuela leaving OPEC earlier this year. However, "it has not been among the issues raised by high-level officials."Washington argued that the money could be used for more important matters instead of paying OPEC dues, one person familiar with Venezuela's relationship with the group told Reuters.OPEC membership fees are usually paid in the first quarter of each year. Each member contributes around 2.8 million euros ($3.08 million) towards the organisation's staff salaries, research and travel expenses.Although the amount is small compared with oil revenues, the payment carries symbolic importance for Venezuela, one of the countries that founded the organisation.OPEC has the discretion to overlook unpaid dues and does not plan to expel Venezuela over the issue, two OPEC sources told Reuters.Iraq asked to consider exit amid US oil investmentsUS officials also encouraged Iraq to leave OPEC during discussions with Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi this summer, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.The discussions came as US oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron were planning major new investments in Iraq.Al-Zaidi later raised the possibility of leaving the group at a government meeting. However, Iraq's oil ministry pushed back against the proposal and convinced him to remain in OPEC. It suggested that the country could instead seek a higher production quota.The issue could resurface, as some members of Iraq's ruling coalition favour leaving OPEC and OPEC+. They view the groups as being dominated by Saudi Arabia and Russia, the sources said.Unlike Venezuela, there is no indication that Washington tried to block Iraq's OPEC membership dues.However, the US has considerable financial leverage over Baghdad as well. Iraq's oil revenues continue to pass through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a system established after the 2003 US invasion.Earlier this year, Washington threatened to restrict Iraq's access to its oil revenues if Baghdad did not reduce Iran's influence in its government.The US State Department said its discussions with Iraq had focused on improving energy infrastructure and increasing oil production and transportation, rather than OPEC membership.Trump's long-running opposition to OPECThe US moves add to the pressure on an organisation that has faced a series of departures in recent years. OPEC has lost four members since 2019, while its share of the global oil market recently hit a low following disruptions caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran, another founding member."The risk of OPEC fracture is rising," Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro, told Reuters.The United Arab Emirates announced its exit from OPEC earlier this year after becoming frustrated with the group's production limits. Angola, Ecuador and Qatar also left in 2024, 2020 and 2019, respectively. There is no indication that the US was involved in those decisions.Founded in Baghdad in September 1960, OPEC was established by Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Venezuela. The five oil-producing countries sought greater control over a global market dominated by a handful of Western oil companies.The organisation now has 11 members and has expanded its influence through OPEC+, an alliance that includes other major producers such as Russia. The group regularly coordinates production levels.Trump has repeatedly criticised OPEC throughout his business and political career, accusing it of operating as a cartel and monopoly that keeps oil prices artificially high.The US has also transformed its position in the global oil market over the past decade. It is now the world's largest oil producer, making it a major competitor to OPEC rather than simply a customer.Venezuela, meanwhile, remains exempt from OPEC+ production quotas as its oil output has fallen sharply after years of sanctions and mismanagement. It produced around 1.2 million barrels per day in September, according to OPEC figures. State oil company PDVSA aims to raise production to 1.5 million barrels per day by the end of next year.The US government accountability office opened a formal investigation in July into the Trump administration's handling and disbursement of Venezuelan oil revenues following requests from lawmakers for greater transparency.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pakistan and Turkey pledge to support Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks under defense pact
articles.summary: ISLAMABAD — Pakistan and Turkey vowed to support Saudi Arabia against ongoing attacks by Houthi rebels as the three nations held talks Friday under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all.
articles.body: ISLAMABAD — Pakistan and Turkey vowed to support Saudi Arabia against ongoing attacks by Houthi rebels as the three nations held talks Friday under a trilateral defense pact that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all. Defense and military officials held more than two hours of talks in Islamabad to discuss developments in the Middle East and pledged to back diplomatic efforts to ease regional tensions, Pakistani officials said. Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in televised remarks said the meeting agreed to continue supporting efforts aimed at de-escalation of regional tensions, and encouraging the peaceful resolution of disputes through dialogue and diplomacy. Dar said the three sides reiterated their condemnation of the attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen that have targeted civilians and civilian infrastructure in the kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The three sides reaffirmed their support for the kingdom “in safeguarding its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity” under the defense pact, Dar said. Pakistan and Turkey say the pact is purely defensive The Pakistani, Turkish and Saudi flags lined the route through Islamabad as vehicles carrying delegates traveled through Islamabad under tight security. Friday’s meeting of the Strategic, Political and Defense Committee falls under the Joint Mecca Defense Agreement, signed in August in the Saudi holy city by Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Turkish officials have said Ankara is considering sending military assistance to Saudi Arabia but insist the Mecca agreement is defensive and that no Turkish troops would be deployed to fight in Yemen or attack the Houthis. Pakistan has also described the agreement as purely defensive, saying it is not directed against any country, including Iran, and reflects a shared desire to strengthen strategic security cooperation. Meanwhile, Erdogan formally approved the three-nation agreement, completing Turkey’s ratification process for the defense pact, according to Turkey’s Official Gazette on Friday. Earlier this month, legislators approved the agreement by 279 votes to 119 in Turkey’s 600-seat parliament, despite objections from opposition parties who had argued that the agreement could embroil Turkey in regional wars and put Turkish soldiers in harm’s way. All three nations want to see an end to the war in Iran In Ankara, Turkish officials said Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defense Minister Yasar Guler and military chief Gen. Selcuk Bayraktaroglu would participate in the meeting. They said Fidan would reaffirm Turkey’s commitment to the agreement and its “full solidarity” with Riyadh. He would also declare unacceptable Houthi attacks that target civilians and civilian infrastructure and threaten regional security. Fidan was also going to stress the importance of pursuing a diplomatic resolution to the conflict between the U.S. and Israel on one side and Iran on the other, and ensuring safe navigation through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, according to an official who requested anonymity to discuss the meeting’s agenda. Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif, Dar and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir attended the meeting. From Saudi Arabia, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and the army chief were present. Asif has said Pakistan will use “whatever means are available” to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Pakistan is also working with countries in the Middle East, including Qatar, to urge the United States and Iran to return to the negotiating table to end the conflict. Pakistan brokered an interim deal between the two sides in June. Authorities declared a local holiday in Islamabad to limit public movement as part of security measures. Traffic police announced road diversions and advised motorists to use alternative routes to accommodate foreign delegations. At a previous meeting in Riyadh, the three sides vowed to immediately implement what they described as their collective defense commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed-upon military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia. Under the agreement, the group’s secretariat has been established in Saudi Arabia, and retired Pakistani Gen. Nauman Mahmood has been selected as its first secretary-general. The pact binds the parties for 10 years, after which they must give three months’ notice to withdraw.

articles.title: At least eight found dead on migrant boat off Spain’s Canary Islands
articles.summary: Six people airlifted to hospital in serious condition, Spanish rescue service says.
articles.body:
At least eight migrants have been found dead on a boat carrying about 100 people that was rescued near Spain’s Canary Islands, the Spanish maritime rescue service has said.

The rescue service said on Friday that between eight and 10 bodies were found on board and that six people were airlifted to hospital in serious condition.

The boat was found 39 nautical miles (72km) south of the island of El Hierro and was being towed to the port of La Estaca.

Separately, 84 survivors from another boat came ashore at La Restinga, El Hierro’s main port, which has a reception centre and field hospital for migrants.

The Canary Islands are a Spanish region in the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of northwest Africa. Anyone who lands there reaches Spanish and European Union territory, which has made the islands a main entry point for migrants from West Africa.

Arrivals hit a record of more than 46,000 in 2024 before falling after tighter surveillance and cooperation with countries of origin and transit.

Patrols off Senegal, Mauritania and Morocco have pushed departures further south to The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau and Guinea, making the crossing longer and more dangerous.

Arrivals in the Canary Islands have accelerated since October, with a record 2,100 people reaching the islands in a single day earlier this week, mostly on El Hierro, which has 11,400 residents.

Authorities there declared an emergency earlier this month, and rescuers brought in nearly 1,500 people in a single day on November 14.

“The humanitarian emergency doesn’t start on El Hierro, but on the shores of Senegal and Gambia, where we have to act,” regional leader Fernando Clavijo said on X.

He expressed “a lot of pain and feeling of impotence” over the deaths and demanded action from the Spanish government and the European Commission.

The deaths come two days before Spain’s general elections on Sunday, in which immigration has become a defining issue.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is one of Europe’s most vocal advocates of the economic benefits of immigration, while the right, which leads in the polls, wants far tighter controls.

Thousands of migrants try the Atlantic crossing each year from West Africa in overcrowded boats, despite rough seas and strong currents.

It is one of the world’s deadliest migration routes, and arrivals usually rise between September and November, when sea conditions are more favourable.

articles.title: Bangladesh hints at ICJ route to bring Hasina back as India examines extradition plea
articles.summary: Bangladesh may approach the International Court of Justice (ICJ) if India refuses to extradite deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina, Parliament Speaker
articles.body: Bangladesh may approach the International Court of Justice (ICJ) if India refuses to extradite deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina, Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmed has said, news agency PTI reported. Ahmed made the remarks during his six-day visit to Pakistan, adding that Hasina would have to go straight to jail if she returned to Bangladesh, BBC Urdu reported on Thursday.Hasina, 79, has been living in India since fleeing Bangladesh in August 2024 following a student-led uprising that toppled her Awami League government. Dhaka has been pursuing her extradition through diplomatic channels. India has acknowledged receiving Bangladesh's requests but has not announced a decision, saying the matter is being examined through established processes.Ahmed also dismissed Hasina's reported plan to return to Bangladesh on December 16, saying the announcement was intended to keep her supporters motivated. He claimed she would not return for the next 10 years.Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali has said the former prime minister plans to return on December 16, the day Bangladesh celebrates its victory over Pakistan in the 1971 Liberation War.Hasina faces serious legal challenges in Bangladesh. A special tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia over the deadly crackdown on protesters during the 2024 uprising. She has denied wrongdoing and questioned the legitimacy of the trial.During his visit to Pakistan, Ahmed also alleged that Bangladesh had effectively become a "colony" of a neighbouring country over the past 15 years, without naming India directly.Ahmed, a former military captain who rebelled against Pakistan during the Liberation War, further alleged that India "did not help the Bengalis but played a role in weakening Pakistan" in 1971. articles.title: Steelers silence the Aaron Rodgers noise, cruise past Broncos to remain perfect at home on Black Friday
articles.summary: T.J. Watt and Jalen Ramsey turned Bo Nix mistakes into touchdowns as the Pittsburgh Steelers snapped Denver's six-game winning streak in the rain.
articles.body: The Pittsburgh Steelers were placed firmly under the microscope this week. Aaron Rodgers’ benching, revealing interview and subsequent departure sent shockwaves through the NFL. Amid the shakeup, coach Mike McCarthy and the Steelers turned their attention to a high-stakes Black Friday matchup with the Denver Broncos. Pittsburgh entered Friday on a two-game losing streak, while Denver had won six straight. But the Steelers embraced the underdog role Friday, upsetting the AFC West-leading Broncos 27-5. Mason Rudolph started at quarterback and threw a touchdown pass, while Pittsburgh’s other stars delivered key plays. T.J. Watt recovered a Bo Nix fumble in the end zone for a touchdown, and Jalen Ramsey intercepted Nix and returned it for another score. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE D.K. Metcalf appeared to show his support for Rodgers after hauling in what was arguably his best catch since joining the Steelers in the first quarter. While celebrating in the end zone, Metcalf signed "stand on business, 8" in American Sign Language. The phrase refers to standing by one’s principles. Rodgers wore No. 8 with the Steelers. While there was still the stray No. 8 jersey in the stands at a rainy Acrisure Stadium, the Steelers began emerging from the rubble behind inspired play from a dominant defense. Nix gifted Pittsburgh an early touchdown when the ball slipped out of his hand on Denver’s second possession and bounced into the end zone while he was pressured by Watt and Nick Herbig. Watt fell on it to send a jolt through the mist. MIKE TOMLIN CALLS STEELERS SITUATION FOLLOWING AARON RODGERS VS. MIKE MCCARTHY FEUD 'A DUMPSTER FIRE' The Kansas City Chiefs’ loss to the Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving night opened the door for the Broncos to take sole possession of first place in the AFC West on Friday. Denver missed the opportunity and will instead settle for a tie at the top of the division standings, at least for now. Save for a second-quarter safety by linebacker Alex Singleton when he tackled running back Jaylen Warren in the Pittsburgh end zone, the Broncos mustered little on a day that in some ways felt like a referendum on the way one of the league’s premier franchises goes about its business. "Earlier today, I heard from Aaron," Michaels said during the broadcast in the fourth quarter. "(He) said, 'A lot of talk about the sanctity of the locker room. The code or sanctity exists to protect the integrity of the locker room, not to provide immunity from accountability for its leadership.'" During a Wednesday interview on "The Pat McAfee Show," Rodgers made a series of allegations about McCarthy’s focus and work ethic. He claimed the coach had been caught "snoring" during team meetings and had recently ended a speech by inadvertently saying, "one, two, three, Packers." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: An Indiana stepfather adopted his wife's nine-year-old daughter after a judge ruled her father's consent unnecessary; on November 25, appeals judges reversed the adoption after finding the mother blocked contact
articles.summary: An Indiana stepfather who adopted his wife’s nine-year-old daughter without the biological father’s consent has had the adoption overturned by an appeals
articles.body: An Indiana stepfather who adopted his wife’s nine-year-old daughter without the biological father’s consent has had the adoption overturned by an appeals court. The court found that the girl’s mother had restricted contact between the child and her biological father, making it wrong to treat his limited communication as grounds for proceeding with the adoption without his approval.In a November 25, 2026, decision, the Indiana Court of Appeals reversed the adoption decree and sent the case back to the lower court. The ruling followed an appeal by the biological father, identified in the judgment as R.R. The mother is identified as J.O., the stepfather as K.N. and the child as M.R.According to the court’s opinion, the girl was born in June 2017. Her biological father was present at her birth and signed a paternity affidavit at the hospital, establishing his legal paternity and parental rights. The mother married K.N. on February 12, 2024. Eight days later, he filed a petition to adopt the child.Why the stepfather sought adoption without the father's consentIn his adoption petition, the stepfather argued that the biological father’s consent was not necessary because he had failed to maintain significant communication with the girl, had not provided adequate financial support and had abandoned her.Under Indiana law, a biological parent's consent may not be required in certain circumstances, according to Law Justia. These include abandoning a child for at least six months or failing, without justifiable cause, to communicate significantly with the child or provide care and support for at least one year when able to do so.The stepfather argued that these conditions applied. The biological father contested the petition. The trial court ruled in favour of the adoption. In an order dated June 25, 2025, it concluded that the father’s contact with the girl was largely token, that he had failed to communicate significantly with her for more than a year and that he had not provided financial support when able to do so. The adoption was formally granted on March 11, 2026.Appeals court found the mother had restricted contactThe biological father challenged the decision, arguing that the trial court had failed to account for the mother's actions in limiting his access to the child. The appeals court examined messages between the mother and the paternal grandmother, who had a close relationship with the girl and regularly spent time with her.According to the judgment, the mother acknowledged that she had told the paternal grandmother in March 2023 that she did not want the child around the biological father. She also admitted telling the grandmother that the child was not to visit the father's home.The appeals court said the mother's own testimony showed that she had worked to restrict and eventually end the father's contact with the child. It found that the trial court's conclusion that she had not obstructed his efforts was unsupported by the evidence.The judges also noted that the mother had not obtained a court order restricting the father's parenting time. The court said a parent cannot unilaterally limit or end the other parent's access and then argue that the other parent failed to communicate without a valid reason.Father had sought legal rights and contributed to expensesThe judgment also examined the biological father's efforts to remain involved in the girl's life. He filed a petition to establish paternity, custody, child support and parenting time on January 22, 2024, less than a month before the stepfather filed the adoption petition.The paternal grandparents testified that the father had contributed towards the child's expenses. The court record referred to payments of $400 a month to the mother in 2020, contributions towards school tuition between January and May 2022, and $500 towards dental expenses in 2023. The father also said he had bought the girl a Nintendo Switch.The grandparents said they had sometimes kept his financial contributions from the mother because they feared she might become upset and stop bringing the child to see them.The appeals court said the trial court had not adequately accounted for this evidence. It also noted that the father had specifically asked for a child support order in his January 2024 petition.One judge disagreed with the decisionThe ruling was not unanimous. Judge Brown wrote the majority opinion, with Judge Scheele concurring. Judge Kenworthy dissented, arguing that the evidence supported the original adoption decision. In the dissenting opinion, Kenworthy said the father had made few direct efforts to arrange parenting time.The judge noted that the parents had discussed a schedule in 2020, but the father had not consistently followed it. He also did not pursue a formal agreement or court order for more than a year after discussing the issue with the mother in January 2023.The dissent said the father's visits were limited and that the paternal grandparents' relationship with the girl could not automatically be treated as communication by the father. The dissent also highlighted the stepfather's role in the child's life.According to the trial court's findings cited in the opinion, he had provided emotional and practical support since 2019, including taking the girl to school and medical appointments, attending school events and sharing household expenses. He also carried her on his health insurance.However, the majority reversed the adoption on the question of the biological father's consent. It said it therefore did not need to decide whether the adoption was in the child's best interests. The case has been sent back to the lower court for further proceedings. The appeals court's decision does not itself determine the child's long-term custody arrangements.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Belgium built a 700-metre circular bicycle path that rises 10 metres into a forest; cyclists can ride through the treetops on a double-loop bridge
articles.summary: A 700-metre circular bicycle path in the Pijnven nature reserve, part of Bosland National Park in the municipality of Hechtel-Eksel, lifts cyclists to 10
articles.body: A 700-metre circular bicycle path in the Pijnven nature reserve, part of Bosland National Park in the municipality of Hechtel-Eksel, lifts cyclists to 10 metres into the treetops. Riders follow a double circle that climbs to its full height, levels out and descends. The path opened in June 2019 and is open to walkers and joggers. Its steel structure earned laureate status in the Steel Construction Contest 2020, in the bridges category. The Pijnven woods around it were planted largely with conifers at the beginning of the last century to supply the mining industry.Where to find the treetop cycle path at node 272 and how to reach it by car or hired bicycleAccording to Visit Limburg, Cycling through the Trees sits at node 272 of the cycle node network in the Pijnven nature reserve. Drivers can use a free car park at Kiefhoekstraat 16 in Hechtel-Eksel. Visitors without their own bicycle can rent one from De Lage Kempen, the nearest rental point, by reserving in advance and collecting it on the day of the visit.Infosteel reports that the route consists of a tight double circle 100 metres in diameter, connected to the cycle network. The path rises at a gradient of three to four per cent, stays level for nine metres once it reaches its full height, and then begins its descent.Its 450 unique columns, made of weather-resistant Corten steel, are spaced one, two and three metres apart in turn. They symbolise the straight trunks of the pine trees that were once used in the mine. The support piles sit on a point foundation of galvanised screw piles, which minimises the structure's impact on the natural environment.Who designed, engineered, checked and built the award-winning steel cycle bridge in Hechtel-EkselTourism Limburg of Hasselt was the client. Burolandschap and De Gregorio & Partners, both of Tongeren, acted as architect and designer, while BAS of Leuven handled the structural engineering. Socotec of Brussels was the control agency, and Smulders of Arendonk served as both general contractor and steel contractor.How the design respects a conifer forest planted for mining and now managed for native treesWhen the mines closed, the trees were never felled. A tailor-made woodland management plan is now giving smaller indigenous trees at the lower levels of the forest more space and light so they can grow. The aim is healthy, balanced forest resources with small, medium-sized and tall trees.Close to the entrance, a cycle pavilion serves as a rest and information point for cyclists and walkers. It is built from two Corten steel frames with logs stacked around them, and the logs come from the trees that were felled to make room for the cycle bridge.The partners behind the project and the other Limburg cycling experiences on the same networkThe project was delivered by Visit Limburg in conjunction with the Province of Limburg, LSM, Visit Flanders, the municipality of Hechtel-Eksel, the Flemish government's Nature and Woodland Agency and Bosland. Cycling through the Trees is not the only attraction on the cycle node network. Two other cycling experiences are Cycling through Water in Bokrijk and Cycling through the Heathland in Hoge Kempen National Park.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
