articles.title: Pete Edochie: How Nigeria's Things Fall Apart star became a Nollywood legend
articles.summary: Before becoming a household name in the Nigerian film industry, Edochie built a career in broadcasting.
articles.body:
For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.

He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.

Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.

Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.

The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.

Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.

She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.

"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.

The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.

"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.

With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.

Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.

Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.

From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.

Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.

Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.

Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.

He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.

He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.

"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.

He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.

His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.

The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.

He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.

His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).

He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.

In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.

His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.

For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.

But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.

Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.

"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.

"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."

Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.

"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.

Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.

"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.

"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."

Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.

"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.

"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."

Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.

The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.

But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.

Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.

"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.

He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.

"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.

Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.

Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.

In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.

It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

articles.title: American Airlines planes clip wings during busy holiday travel weekend at Reagan National in DC
articles.summary: The FAA will investigate after two American Airlines Boeing 737s clipped wings at Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., sending both back to gates.
articles.body: Federal authorities are investigating after two American Airlines Boeing 737-800s clipped wings as they taxied for takeoff Friday at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) in Washington, D.C., forcing both aircraft to return to their gates. The Federal Aviation Administration told Fox News Digital American Airlines Flight 638, bound for Dallas, clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152, headed to Chicago, while waiting in the departure queue at about 5:10 p.m. Both planes returned to their gates and were checked by Airports Authority Fire and Rescue personnel, according to the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority. UPS CARGO PLANE, COPA AIRLINES PASSENGER JET COLLIDE AT MIAMI AIRPORT, LEAVING 2 INJURED American Airlines told Fox News Digital there were no injuries, and both aircraft have been removed from service for inspection by its maintenance team. "We apologize to our customers for the inconvenience and are working to get them on their way as soon as possible," American Airlines wrote in a statement. REAGAN NATIONAL AIRPORT MAKES DRASTIC CHANGE FOLLOWING DEADLY 2025 MIDAIR COLLISION The MWAA said no other flights were disrupted during the busy holiday weekend, and the airline noted customers from both flights will re-depart Friday evening. The FAA will investigate the incident. A similar incident occurred at DCA in April 2025, when another plane bumped the wing of an aircraft carrying several U.S. lawmakers and two former Gaza hostages as it waited to take off. Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital at the time that he was on the plane alongside Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., Richie Torres, D-N.Y., and Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y. No injuries were reported. "Serving in Congress has come with some once in a lifetime experiences… like just now while stationary on the runway at DCA, another plane just bumped into our wing," LaLota wrote in a social media post shortly after the collision. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Both planes involved in the April 2025 collision were operated by American Airlines, Fox News Digital previously reported. "Congressman LaLota intends to bring this firsthand experience to his work in Congress, advocating for stronger aviation oversight and enhanced public safety to help prevent similar incidents in the future," LaLota's office told Fox News Digital at the time.

articles.title: Italy bans burqas, niqabs in schools; caps foreign students at 30% in classrooms
articles.summary: Italy has approved a controversial education reform introducing a ban on face coverings in schools and a 30 per cent cap on students of foreign origin in
articles.body: Italy has approved a controversial education reform introducing a ban on face coverings in schools and a 30 per cent cap on students of foreign origin in first-year classes, drawing accusations of discrimination from opposition parties.The reform, approved by the Chamber of Deputies with 142 votes in favour, 112 against and four abstentions, also introduces Italian language courses for foreign parents whose children face difficulties integrating into the country's education system.The legislation, known as the Decreto Scuola, had earlier been approved by the Senate on November 20. It is part of Decree-law 170 of September 30, 2026, which introduces measures to ensure the regular start of the 2026-27 academic year, support initiatives under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) and promote the integration of foreign students.The new rules will prevent Muslim female students from wearing burqas and niqabs in classrooms. However, the 30 per cent cap on students of foreign origin will not apply to those who have already acquired an adequate knowledge of Italian.The final vote in the lower house was marked by protests from opposition lawmakers, who displayed a sign reading "At school nobody is a foreigner" in the chamber.What the new education reform proposesThe 30 per cent limit on non-Italian students is not entirely new. A similar restriction was introduced through a 2010 ministerial circular issued by then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini. However, it has often gone unenforced because of local demographic conditions and a lack of flexibility, particularly in urban outskirts.The latest legislation also provides for Italian language courses for foreign parents, particularly those whose children face serious difficulties integrating into the national school system.Earlier this year, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced that her government was preparing legislation to ban burqas and niqabs in schools, restrict the number of foreign students in classrooms and require parents of children facing integration difficulties to learn Italian.At a rally organised by Gioventù Nazionale, the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy party, Meloni defended the proposed restrictions, arguing that Italian students should not become minorities in their own classrooms.“It is unacceptable that in an Italian classroom the children who end up feeling pushed into a corner are Italian children because they have become the minority. That cannot be allowed,” she said.“Calling all this integration is yet another lie, a convenient lie for those who live off ideology, for those who preach to us from their living rooms and then send their own children to schools where this problem does not exist.”Growing restrictions on face coverings across EuropeItaly's move comes amid wider restrictions on face coverings across several European countries. France and Belgium have already introduced nationwide bans on concealing the face in public places, while Austria has imposed restrictions in educational institutions.The Italian legislation specifically targets burqas and niqabs. A burqa traditionally covers the entire body, including the eyes with a mesh screen, while a niqab covers the face, leaving only the eyes visible. A hijab, in contrast, covers the hair and neck but leaves the face uncovered.France introduced a nationwide ban on concealing the face in public places in April 2011, a measure subsequently upheld by the European Court of Human Rights. Belgium followed with a similar ban in July 2011, prescribing fines and prison sentences for violations.Bulgaria has prohibited full-face veils in state, administrative and educational institutions since September 2016. Austria introduced an anti-mask law in October 2017, requiring faces to remain visible in public spaces. From September 2026, girls up to the age of 14 will also be prohibited from wearing veils covering the head according to Islamic traditions in schools.Denmark introduced a nationwide ban in August 2018, with financial penalties increasing for repeat violations. The Netherlands followed in August 2019 with a partial ban covering schools, hospitals, government offices and public transport.Switzerland introduced a federal ban on face coverings in public spaces following a national referendum, with the implementing legislation taking effect in 2023. Portugal completed its legislative process in August 2026 with a law prohibiting face coverings in public spaces and prescribing financial penalties.Germany, meanwhile, has no nationwide ban but has restrictions on face coverings for public employees, judges, members of the armed forces and motorists. Several German states also restrict full-face veils in schools and universities for students and teachers.Migration debate intensifies ahead of electionsThe reform comes as migration remains a divisive political issue in Italy, with the country scheduled to hold elections next year.Competition to the right of Meloni's party has intensified following the entry of retired general Roberto Vannacci into the political arena. Vannacci has advocated even tougher measures on migration.Meloni's government has increasingly placed integration and restrictions on migration at the centre of its political agenda, with the latest education reform bringing these issues into the country's school system.You use AI every day.
